entries.ae7841c2c9d79582208bd662aa96e22412f70ecf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19049"/><div sID="gen41214" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19049"/><hi type="bold">2. bare record of--</hi>"testified the word of God" in this book. Where we would say "testifies," the ancients in epistolary communications use the past tense. The word of God constitutes his testimony; <reference osisRef="Rev.1.3">Re 1:3</reference>, "the words of this prophecy."<div eID="gen41214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41215" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the testimony of Jesus--</hi>"the Spirit of prophecy" (<reference osisRef="Rev.19.10">Re 19:10</reference>).<div eID="gen41215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41216" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and of all things that, &c.--</hi>The oldest manuscripts omit "and." Translate, "whatsoever things he saw," in apposition with "the word of God and the testimony of Jesus Christ." <div eID="gen41216" type="x-p"/>
entries.3d97d4581bc6b511bac7ee9dc24056bd30b90519: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19050"/><div sID="gen41217" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19050"/><hi type="bold">3. he that readeth, and they that hear--</hi>namely, the public reader in Church assemblies, and his hearers. In the first instance, he by whom John sent the book from Patmos to the seven churches, read it publicly: a usage most scriptural and profitable. A special blessing attends him who reads or hears the apocalyptic "prophecy" with a view to keeping the things therein (as there is but one article to "they that hear and keep those things," not two classes, but only one is meant: "they who not only hear, but also keep those things," <reference osisRef="Rom.2.13">Ro 2:13</reference>); even though he find not the key to its interpretation, he finds a stimulus to faith, hope, and patient waiting for Christ. Note: the term "prophecy" has relation to the human medium or prophet inspired, here John: "Revelation" to the Divine Being who reveals His will, here Jesus Christ. God gave the revelation to Jesus: He by His angel revealed it to John, who was to make it known to the Church. <div eID="gen41217" type="x-p"/>
entries.f9ae4f9d7f2cf9eedf16d32d978ba75d02c6dd43: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19051"/><div sID="gen41218" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19051"/><hi type="bold">4. John--</hi>the apostle. For none but he (supposing the writer an honest man) would thus sign himself nakedly without addition. As sole survivor and representative of the apostles and eye-witnesses of the Lord, he needed no designation save his name, to be recognized by his readers.<div eID="gen41218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41219" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seven churches--</hi>not that there were not more churches in that region, but the number seven is fixed on as representing totality. These seven represent the universal Church of all times and places. See Trench's [Commentary on the Epistles to the Seven Churches in Asia] interesting note, <reference osisRef="Rev.1.20">Re 1:20</reference>, on the number seven. It is the covenant number, the sign of God's covenant relation to mankind, and especially to the Church. Thus, the seventh day, sabbath (<reference osisRef="Gen.2.3">Ge 2:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.12">Eze 20:12</reference>). Circumcision, the sign of the covenant, after seven days (<reference osisRef="Gen.17.12">Ge 17:12</reference>). Sacrifices (<reference osisRef="Num.23.1">Nu 23:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.14.29">14:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.29.21">2Ch 29:21</reference>). Compare also God's acts typical of His covenant (<reference osisRef="Josh.6.4">Jos 6:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.15.16">15, 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.5.10">2Ki 5:10</reference>). The feasts ordered by sevens of time (<reference osisRef="Deut.15.1">De 15:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.16.9">16:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.13.15">13, 15</reference>). It is a combination of three, the divine number (thus the Trinity: the thrice Holy, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.3">Is 6:3</reference>; the blessing, <reference osisRef="Num.6.24-Num.6.26">Nu 6:24-26</reference>), and four the number of the organized world in its extension (thus the four elements, the four seasons, the four winds, the four corners or quarters of the earth, the four living creatures, emblems of redeemed creaturely life, <reference osisRef="Rev.4.6">Re 4:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.1.5">Eze 1:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.6">6</reference>, with four faces and four wings each; the four beasts and four metals, representing the four world empires, <reference osisRef="Dan.2.32">Da 2:32</reference>, 33; <reference osisRef="2Cor.7.3">7:3</reference>; the four-sided Gospel designed for all quarters of the world; the sheet tied at four corners, <reference osisRef="Acts.10.11">Ac 10:11</reference>; the four horns, the sum of the world's forces against the Church, <reference osisRef="Zech.1.18">Zec 1:18</reference>). In the Apocalypse, where God's covenant with His Church comes to its consummation, appropriately the number seven recurs still more frequently than elsewhere in Scripture.<div eID="gen41219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41220" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Asia--</hi>Proconsular, governed by a Roman proconsul: consisting of Phrygia, Mysia, Caria, and Lydia: the kingdom which Attalus III had bequeathed to Rome.<div eID="gen41220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41221" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Grace ... peace--</hi>Paul's apostolical greeting. In his Pastoral Epistles he inserts "mercy" in addition: so 2Jo 3.<div eID="gen41221" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41222" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">him which is ... was ... is to come--</hi>a periphrasis for the incommunicable name Jehovah, the self-existing One, unchangeable. In Greek the indeclinability of the designation here implies His unchangeableness. Perhaps the reason why "He which is to come" is used, instead of "He that shall be," is because the grand theme of Revelation is the Lord's coming (<reference osisRef="Rev.1.7">Re 1:7</reference>). Still it is THE Father as distinguished from "Jesus Christ" (<reference osisRef="Rev.1.5">Re 1:5</reference>) who is here meant. But so one are the Father and Son that the designation, "which is to come," more immediately applicable to Christ, is used here of the Father.<div eID="gen41222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41223" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the seven Spirits which are before his throne--</hi>The oldest manuscripts omit "are."<div eID="gen41223" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41224" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">before--</hi>literally, "in the presence of." The Holy Spirit in His sevenfold (that is, perfect, complete, and universal) energy. Corresponding to "the seven churches." One in His own essence, manifold in His gracious influences. The seven eyes resting on the stone laid by Jehovah (<reference osisRef="Rev.5.6">Re 5:6</reference>). Four is the number of the creature world (compare the fourfold cherubim); seven the number of God's revelation in the world. <div eID="gen41224" type="x-p"/>
entries.9aba6e81fa6ab3d1d3910cf3abe50530393c3c15: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19052"/><div sID="gen41225" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19052"/><hi type="bold">5. the faithful witness--</hi>of the truth concerning Himself and His mission as Prophet, Priest, and King Saviour. "He was the faithful witness, because all things that He heard of the Father He faithfully made known to His disciples. Also, because He taught the way of God in truth, and cared not for man, nor regarded the persons of men. Also, because the truth which He taught in words He confirmed by miracles. Also, because the testimony to Himself on the part of the Father He denied not even in death. Lastly, because He will give true testimony of the works of good and bad at the day of judgment" [Richard of St. Victor in Trench]. The nominative in Greek standing in apposition to the genitive, "Jesus Christ," gives majestic prominence to "the faithful witness."<div eID="gen41225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41226" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the first-begotten of the dead--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Col.1.18">Col 1:18</reference>). Lazarus rose, to die again. Christ rose to die no more. The image is not as if the grave was the womb of His resurrection-birth [Alford]; but as <reference osisRef="Acts.13.33">Ac 13:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.1.4">Ro 1:4</reference>, treat Christ's resurrection as the epoch and event which fulfilled the Scripture, <reference osisRef="Ps.2.7">Psa 2:7</reference>, "This day (at the resurrection) have I begotten Thee." It was then that His divine Sonship as the God-man was manifested and openly attested by the Father. So our resurrection and our manifested sonship, or generation, are connected. Hence "regeneration" is used of the resurrection-state at the restitution of all things (<reference osisRef="Matt.19.28">Mt 19:28</reference>).<div eID="gen41226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41227" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the prince--</hi>or Ruler. The kingship of the world which the tempter offered to Jesus on condition of doing homage to him, and so shunning the cross, He has obtained by the cross. "The kings of the earth" conspired against the Lord's Anointed (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.2">Psa 2:2</reference>): these He shall break in pieces (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.9">Psa 2:9</reference>). Those who are wise in time and kiss the Son shall bring their glory unto Him at His manifestation as King of kings, after He has destroyed His foes.<div eID="gen41227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41228" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Unto him that loved us--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read the present, "... loveth us." It is His ever-continuing character, He loveth us, and ever shall love us. His love rests evermore on His people.<div eID="gen41228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41229" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">washed us--</hi>The two oldest manuscripts read, "freed (loosed as from a bond) us": so Andreas and Primasius. One very old manuscript, Vulgate, and Coptic read as English Version, perhaps drawn from <reference osisRef="Rev.7.4">Re 7:4</reference>. "Loosed us in (virtue of) His blood," being the harder reading to understand, is less likely to have come from the transcribers. The reference is thus to Greek, "lutron," the ransom paid for our release (<reference osisRef="Matt.20.28">Mt 20:28</reference>). In favor of English Version reading is the usage whereby the priests, before putting on the holy garments and ministering, washed themselves: so spiritually believers, as priests unto God, must first be washed in Christ's blood from every stain before they can serve God aright now, or hereafter minister as dispensers of blessing to the subject nations in the millennial kingdom, or minister before God in heaven. <div eID="gen41229" type="x-p"/>
entries.de141d7e1f3ac167cb05e5760954116089ebe210: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19053"/><div sID="gen41230" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19053"/><hi type="bold">6. And hath--</hi>rather as Greek, "And (He) hath."<div eID="gen41230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41231" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">made us kings--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read, "a kingdom." One oldest manuscript reads the dative, "for us." Another reads "us," accusative: so Vulgate, Syriac, Coptic, and Andreas. This seems preferable, "He made us (to be) a kingdom." So <reference osisRef="Exod.19.6">Ex 19:6</reference>, "a kingdom of priests"; <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.9">1Pe 2:9</reference>, "a royal priesthood." The saints shall constitute peculiarly a kingdom of God, and shall themselves be kings (<reference osisRef="Rev.5.10">Re 5:10</reference>). They shall share His King-Priest throne in the millennial kingdom. The emphasis thus falls more on the kingdom than on priests: whereas in English Version reading it is equally distributed between both. This book lays prominent stress on the saints' kingdom. They are kings because they are priests: the priesthood is the continuous ground and legitimization of their kingship; they are kings in relation to man, priests in relation to God, serving Him day and night in His temple (<reference osisRef="Rev.7.15">Re 7:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.5.10">5:10</reference>). The priest-kings shall rule, not in an external mechanical manner, but simply in virtue of what they are, by the power of attraction and conviction overcoming the heart [Auberlen].<div eID="gen41231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41232" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">priests--</hi>who have pre-eminently the privilege of near access to the king. David's sons were priests (Hebrew), <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.18">2Sa 8:18</reference>. The distinction of priests and people, nearer and more remote from God, shall cease; all shall have nearest access to Him. All persons and things shall be holy to the Lord.<div eID="gen41232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41233" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">God and his Father--</hi>There is but one article to both in the Greek, therefore it means, "Unto Him who is at once God and His Father."<div eID="gen41233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41234" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">glory and dominion--</hi>Greek, "the glory and the might." The fuller threefold doxology occurs, <reference osisRef="Rev.4.9">Re 4:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.4.11">11</reference>; fourfold, <reference osisRef="Rev.5.13">Re 5:13</reference>; Jude 25; sevenfold, <reference osisRef="Rev.7.12">Re 7:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.11">1Ch 29:11</reference>. Doxology occupies the prominent place above, which prayer does below. If we thought of God's glory first (as in the Lord's Prayer), and gave the secondary place to our needs, we should please God and gain our petitions better than we do.<div eID="gen41234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41235" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for ever and ever--</hi>Greek, "unto the ages." <div eID="gen41235" type="x-p"/>
entries.4ed0e3e5f75052d3bd93faf2daf55180b9081bc9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19054"/><div sID="gen41236" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19054"/><hi type="bold">7. with clouds--</hi>Greek, "the clouds," namely, of heaven. "A cloud received Him out of their sight" at His ascension (<reference osisRef="Acts.1.9">Ac 1:9</reference>). His ascension corresponds to the manner of His coming again (<reference osisRef="Acts.1.11">Ac 1:11</reference>). Clouds are the symbols of wrath to sinners.<div eID="gen41236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41237" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">every eye--</hi>His coming shall therefore be a personal, visible appearing.<div eID="gen41237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41238" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall see--</hi>It is because they do not now see Him, they will not believe. Contrast <reference osisRef="John.20.29">Joh 20:29</reference>.<div eID="gen41238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41239" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they also--</hi>they in particular; "whosoever." Primarily, at His pre-millennial advent the Jews, who shall "look upon Him whom they have pierced," and mourn in repentance, and say, "Blessed is He that cometh in the name of the Lord." Secondarily, and here chiefly, at the general judgment all the ungodly, not only those who actually pierced Him, but those who did so by their sins, shall look with trembling upon Him. John is the only one of the Evangelists who records the piercing of Christ's side. This allusion identifies him as the author of the Apocalypse. The reality of Christ's humanity and His death is proved by His having been pierced; and the water and blood from His side were the antitype to the Levitical waters of cleansing and blood offerings.<div eID="gen41239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41240" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all kindreds ... shall wail--</hi>all the unconverted at the general judgment; and especially at His pre-millennial advent, the Antichristian confederacy (<reference osisRef="Zech.12.3-Zech.6.9">Zec 12:3-6, 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.14.1-Zech.14.4">14:1-4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.24.30">Mt 24:30</reference>). Greek, "all the tribes of the land," or "the earth." See the limitation to "all," <reference osisRef="Rev.13.8">Re 13:8</reference>. Even the godly while rejoicing in His love shall feel penitential sorrow at their sins, which shall all be manifested at the general judgment.<div eID="gen41240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41241" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">because of--</hi>Greek, "at," or "in regard to Him."<div eID="gen41241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41242" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Even so, Amen--</hi>Gods seal of His own word; to which corresponds the believer's prayer, <reference osisRef="Rev.22.20">Re 22:20</reference>. The "even so" is Greek; "Amen" is Hebrew. To both Gentiles and Jews His promises and threats are unchangeable. <div eID="gen41242" type="x-p"/>
entries.5a312326061b5e80ad64205e5d90d4ec4e730f50: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19055"/><div sID="gen41243" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19055"/>8. Greek, "I am the Alpha and the Omega." The first and last letters of the alphabet. God in Christ comprises all that goes between, as well as the first and last.<div eID="gen41243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41244" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the beginning and the ending--</hi>omitted in the oldest manuscripts, though found in Vulgate and Coptic. Transcribers probably inserted the clause from <reference osisRef="Rev.21.6">Re 21:6</reference>. In Christ, Genesis, the Alpha of the Old Testament, and Revelation, the Omega of the New Testament, meet together: the last book presenting to us man and God reconciled in Paradise, as the first book presented man at the beginning innocent and in God's favor in Paradise. Accomplishing finally what I begin. Always the same; before the dragon, the beast, false prophet, and all foes. An anticipatory consolation to the saints under the coming trials of the Church.<div eID="gen41244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41245" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the Lord--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read "the Lord God."<div eID="gen41245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41246" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Almighty--</hi>Hebrew, "Shaddai," and "Jehovah Sabaoth," that is, "of hosts"; commanding all the hosts or powers in heaven and earth, so able to overcome all His Church's foes. It occurs often in Revelation, but nowhere else in the New Testament save <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.18">2Co 6:18</reference>, a quotation from Isaiah. <div eID="gen41246" type="x-p"/>
entries.2f23c61f5f6dae134ba51b40913d6407bac47d9c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19056"/><div sID="gen41247" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19056"/><hi type="bold">9. I John--</hi>So "I Daniel" (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.28">Da 7:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.9.2">9:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.10.2">10:2</reference>). One of the many features of resemblance between the Old Testament and the New Testament apocalyptic seers. No other Scripture writer uses the phrase.<div eID="gen41247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41248" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">also--</hi>as well as being an apostle. The oldest manuscripts omit "also." In his Gospel and Epistles he makes no mention of his name, though describing himself as "the disciple whom Jesus loved." Here, with similar humility, though naming himself, he does not mention his apostleship.<div eID="gen41248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41249" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">companion--</hi>Greek, "fellow partaker in the tribulation." Tribulation is the necessary precursor of the kingdom," therefore "the" is prefixed. This must be borne with "patient endurance." The oldest manuscripts omit "in the" before "kingdom." All three are inseparable: the tribulation, kingdom and endurance.<div eID="gen41249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41250" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">patience--</hi>Translate, "endurance." "Persevering, enduring continuance" (<reference osisRef="Acts.14.22">Ac 14:22</reference>); "the queen of the graces (virtues)" [Chrysostom].<div eID="gen41250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41251" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of, &c.--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read "IN Jesus," or "Jesus Christ." It is IN Him that believers have the right to the kingdom, and the spiritual strength to enable them to endure patiently for it.<div eID="gen41251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41252" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">was--</hi>Greek, "came to be."<div eID="gen41252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41253" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in ... Patmos--</hi>now Patmo or Palmosa. See Introduction on this island, and John's exile to it under Domitian, from which he was released under Nerva. Restricted to a small spot on earth, he is permitted to penetrate the wide realms of heaven and its secrets. Thus John drank of Christ's cup, and was baptized with His baptism (<reference osisRef="Matt.20.22">Mt 20:22</reference>).<div eID="gen41253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41254" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for--</hi>Greek, "for the sake of," "on account of"; so, "because of the word of God and ... testimony." Two oldest manuscripts omit the second "for"; thus "the Word of God" and "testimony of Jesus" are the more closely joined. Two oldest manuscripts omit "Christ." The Apocalypse has been always appreciated most by the Church in adversity. Thus the Asiatic Church from the flourishing times of Constantine less estimated it. The African Church being more exposed to the cross always made much of it [Bengel]. <div eID="gen41254" type="x-p"/>
entries.11673734b85a2c84c2e9dbda38c89c0e21049624: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19057"/><div sID="gen41255" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19057"/><hi type="bold">10. I was--</hi>Greek, "I came to be"; "I became."<div eID="gen41255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41256" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the Spirit--</hi>in a state of ecstasy; the outer world being shut out, and the inner and higher life or spirit being taken full possession of by God's Spirit, so that an immediate connection with the invisible world is established. While the prophet "speaks" in the Spirit, the apocalyptic seer is in the Spirit in his whole person. The spirit only (that which connects us with God and the invisible world) is active, or rather recipient, in the apocalyptic state. With Christ this being "in the Spirit" was not the exception, but His continual state.<div eID="gen41256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41257" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">on the Lord's day--</hi>Though forcibly detained from Church communion with the brethren in the sanctuary on the Lord's day, the weekly commemoration of the resurrection, John was holding spiritual communion with them. This is the earliest mention of the term, "the Lord's day." But the consecration of the day to worship, almsgiving, and the Lord's Supper, is implied in <reference osisRef="Acts.20.7">Ac 20:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.2">1Co 16:2</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="John.20.19-John.20.26">Joh 20:19-26</reference>. The name corresponds to "the Lord's Supper," <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.20">1Co 11:20</reference>. Ignatius seems to allude to "the Lord's day" [Epistle to the Magnesians, 9], and Irenæus [Quæst ad Orthod., 115] (in Justin Martyr). Justin Martyr [Apology, 2.98], &c., "On Sunday we all hold our joint meeting; for the first day is that on which God, having removed darkness and chaos, made the world, and Jesus Christ our Saviour rose from the dead. On the day before Saturday they crucified Him; and on the day after Saturday, which is Sunday, having appeared to His apostles and disciples, He taught these things." To the Lord's day Pliny doubtless refers [Epistles, Book X., p. 97], "The Christians on a fixed day before dawn meet and sing a hymn to Christ as God," &c. Tertullian [The Chaplet, 3], "On the Lord's day we deem it wrong to fast." Melito, bishop of Sardis (second century), wrote a book on the Lord's day [Eusebius 4.26]. Also, Dionysius of Corinth, in Eusebius [Ecclesiastical History, 4.23,8]. Clement of Alexandria [Miscellanies, 5. and 7.12]; Origen [Against Celsus, 8. 22]. The theory that the day of Christ's second coming is meant, is untenable. "The day of the Lord" is different in the Greek from "the Lord's (an adjective) day," which latter in the ancient Church always designates our Sunday, though it is not impossible that the two shall coincide (at least in some parts of the earth), whence a tradition is mentioned in Jerome [Commentary on Matthew, 25], that the Lord's coming was expected especially on the Paschal Lord's day. The visions of the Apocalypse, the seals, trumpets, and vials, &c., are grouped in sevens, and naturally begin on the first day of the seven, the birthday of the Church, whose future they set forth [Wordsworth].<div eID="gen41257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41258" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">great voice--</hi>summoning solemn attention; Greek order, "I heard a voice behind me great (loud) as (that) of a trumpet." The trumpet summoned to religious feasts, and accompanies God's revelations of Himself. <div eID="gen41258" type="x-p"/>
entries.a48a563a8fb92256f082a02fa6692a8c3bd02c00: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19058"/><div sID="gen41259" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19058"/><hi type="bold">11. I am Alpha and Omega, the first and the last; and--</hi>The oldest manuscripts, omit all this clause.<div eID="gen41259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41260" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">write in a book--</hi>To this book, having such an origin, and to the other books of Holy Scripture, who is there that gives the weight which their importance demands, preferring them to the many books of the world? [Bengel].<div eID="gen41260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41261" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seven churches--</hi>As there were many other churches in Proconsular Asia (for example, Miletus, Magnesia, Tralles), besides the seven specified, doubtless the number seven is fixed upon because of its mystical signification, expressing totality and universality. The words, "which are in Asia" are rejected by the oldest manuscripts, A, B, C, Cyprian, Vulgate, and Syriac; Coptic alone supports them of old authorities. These seven are representative churches; and, as a complex whole, ideally complete, embody the chief spiritual characteristics of the Church, whether as faithful or unfaithful, in all ages. The churches selected are not taken at random, but have a many-sided completeness. Thus, on one side we have Smyrna, a Church exposed to persecutions unto death; on the other Sardis, having a high name for spiritual life and yet dead. Again, Laodicea, in its own estimate rich and having need of nothing, with ample talents, yet lukewarm in Christ's cause; on the other hand, Philadelphia, with but a little strength, yet keeping Christ's word and having an open door of usefulness set before it by Christ Himself. Again, Ephesus, intolerant of evil and of false apostles, yet having left its first love; on the other hand, Thyatira, abounding in works, love, service, and faith, yet suffering the false prophetess to seduce many. In another aspect, Ephesus in conflict with false freedom, that is fleshly licentiousness (the Nicolaitanes); so also Pergamos in conflict with Balaam-like tempters to fornication and idol-meats; and on the other side, Philadelphia in conflict with the Jewish synagogue, that is, legal bondage. Finally, Sardis and Laodicea without any active opposition to call forth their spiritual energies; a dangerous position, considering man's natural indolence. In the historic scheme of interpretation, which seems fanciful, Ephesus (meaning "the beloved" or "desired" [Stier]) represents the waning period of the apostolic age. Smyrna ("myrrh"), bitter suffering, yet sweet and costly perfume, the martyr period of the Decian and Diocletian age. Pergamos (a "castle" or "tower"), the Church possessing earthly power and decreasing spirituality from Constantine's time until the seventh century. Thyatira ("unwearied about sacrifices"), the Papal Church in the first half of the Middle Ages; like "Jezebel," keen about its so-called sacrifice of the mass, and slaying the prophets and witnesses of God. Sardis, from the close of the twelfth century to the Reformation. Philadelphia ("brotherly love"), the first century of the Reformation. Laodicea, the Reformed Church after its first zeal had become lukewarm. <div eID="gen41261" type="x-p"/>
entries.a020ee38255fb9e3a058f9c5247cbfc31b30a39f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19059"/><div sID="gen41262" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19059"/><hi type="bold">12. see the voice--</hi>that is, ascertain whence the voice came; to see who was it from whom the voice proceeded.<div eID="gen41262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41263" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that--</hi>Greek, "of what kind it was which." The voice is that of God the Father, as at Christ's baptism and transfiguration, so here in presenting Christ as our High Priest.<div eID="gen41263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41264" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">spake--</hi>The oldest manuscripts, versions, and Fathers read, "was speaking."<div eID="gen41264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41265" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">being--</hi>"having turned."<div eID="gen41265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41266" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seven ... candlesticks--</hi>"lamp-stands" [Kelly]. The stand holding the lamp. In <reference osisRef="Exod.25.31">Ex 25:31</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.25.32">32</reference>, the seven are united in ONE candlestick or lamp-stand, that is, six arms and a central shaft; so <reference osisRef="Zech.4.2">Zec 4:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.4.11">11</reference>. Here the seven are separate candlesticks, typifying, as that one, the entire Church, but now no longer as the Jewish Church (represented by the one sevenfold candlestick) restricted to one outward unity and one place; the several churches are mutually independent as to external ceremonies and government (provided all things are done to edification, and schisms or needless separations are avoided), yet one in the unity of the Spirit and the Headship of Christ. The candlestick is not light, but the bearer of light, holding it forth to give light around. The light is the Lord's, not the Church's; from Him she receives it. She is to be a light-bearer to His glory. The candlestick stood in the holy place, the type of the Church on earth, as the holiest place was type of the Church in heaven. The holy place's only light was derived from the candlestick, daylight being excluded; so the Lord God is the Church's only light; hers is the light of grace, not nature. "Golden" symbolizes at once the greatest preciousness and sacredness; so that in the Zend Avesta, "golden" is synonymous with heavenly or divine [Trench]. <div eID="gen41266" type="x-p"/>
entries.3f2be8b263bce8852124733d3c2cbfb76d8b57e6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19060"/><div sID="gen41267" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19060"/>13. His glorified form as man could be recognized by John, who had seen it at the Transfiguration.<div eID="gen41267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41268" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the midst--</hi>implying Christ's continual presence and ceaseless activity in the midst of His people on earth. In <reference osisRef="Rev.4.1-Rev.4.3">Re 4:1-3</reference>, when He appears in heaven, His insignia undergo a corresponding change yet even there the rainbow reminds us of His everlasting covenant with them.<div eID="gen41268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41269" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seven--</hi>omitted in two of the oldest manuscripts, but supported by one.<div eID="gen41269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41270" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Son of man--</hi>The form which John had seen enduring the agony of Gethsemane, and the shame and anguish of Calvary, he now sees glorified. His glory (as Son of man, not merely Son of God) is the result of His humiliation as Son of man.<div eID="gen41270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41271" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">down to the foot--</hi>a mark of high rank. The garment and girdle seem to be emblems of His priesthood. Compare <reference osisRef="Exod.28.2">Ex 28:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.4.31">4, 31</reference>; Septuagint. Aaron's robe and girdle were "for glory and beauty," and combined the insignia of royalty and priesthood, the characteristics of Christ's antitypical priesthood "after the order of Melchisedec." His being in the midst of the candlesticks (only seen in the temple), shows that it is as a king-priest He is so attired. This priesthood He has exercised ever since His ascension; and, therefore He here wears its emblems. As Aaron wore these insignia when He came forth from the sanctuary to bless the people (<reference osisRef="Lev.16.4">Le 16:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.24">23, 24</reference>, the chetoneth, or holy linen coat), so when Christ shall come again, He shall appear in the similar attire of "beauty and glory" (<reference osisRef="Isa.4.2">Is 4:2</reference>, Margin). The angels are attired somewhat like their Lord (<reference osisRef="Rev.15.6">Re 15:6</reference>). The ordinary girding for one actively engaged, was at the loins; but Josephus [Antiquities,3.7.2], expressly tells us that the Levitical priests were girt higher up, about the breasts or paps, appropriate to calm, majestic movement. The girdle bracing the frame together, symbolizes collected powers. Righteousness and faithfulness are Christ's girdle. The high priest's girdle was only interwoven with gold, but Christ's is all of gold; the antitype exceeds the type.<div eID="gen41271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41272" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">14.--</hi>Greek, "But," or "And."<div eID="gen41272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41273" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">like wool--</hi>Greek, "like white wool." The color is the point of comparison; signifying purity and glory. (So in <reference osisRef="Isa.1.18">Is 1:18</reference>). Not age, for hoary hairs are the sign of decay.<div eID="gen41273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41274" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">eyes ... as ... flame--</hi>all-searching and penetrating like fire: at the same time, also, implying consuming indignation against sin, especially at His coming "in flaming fire, taking vengeance" on all the ungodly, which is confirmed as the meaning here, by <reference osisRef="Rev.19.11">Re 19:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.12">12</reference>. <div eID="gen41274" type="x-p"/>
entries.9eac69964c59c8f5d9cf1da78c67aed47cca4c12: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19061"/><div sID="gen41275" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19061"/><hi type="bold">15. fine brass--</hi>Greek, "chalcolibanus," derived by some from two Greek words, "brass" and "frankincense"; derived by Bochart from Greek, "chalcos," "brass," and Hebrew, "libbeen," "to whiten"; hence, "brass," which in the furnace has reached a white heat. Thus it answers to "burnished (flashing, or glowing) brass," <reference osisRef="Ezek.1.7">Eze 1:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.10.1">Re 10:1</reference>, "His feet as pillars of fire." Translate, "Glowing brass, as if they had been made fiery (red-hot) in a furnace." The feet of the priests were bare in ministering in the sanctuary. So our great High Priest here.<div eID="gen41275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41276" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">voice as ... many waters--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.43.2">Eze 43:2</reference>); in <reference osisRef="Dan.10.6">Da 10:6</reference>, it is "like the voice of a multitude." As the Bridegroom's voice, so the bride's, <reference osisRef="Rev.14.2">Re 14:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.19.6">19:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.1.24">Eze 1:24</reference>, the cherubim, or redeemed creation. His voice, however, is here regarded in its terribleness to His foes. Contrast <reference osisRef="Song.2.8">So 2:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.2">5:2</reference>, with which compare <reference osisRef="Rev.3.20">Re 3:20</reference>. <div eID="gen41276" type="x-p"/>
entries.001ec48be2a69cf913e2cc7d9ef00946016df1a6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19062"/><div sID="gen41277" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19062"/><hi type="bold">16. he had--</hi>Greek, "having." John takes up the description from time to time, irrespective of the construction, with separate strokes of the pencil [Alford].<div eID="gen41277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41278" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in ... right hand seven stars--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Rev.1.20">Re 1:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.2.1">Re 2:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.1">3:1</reference>). He holds them as a star-studded "crown of glory," or "royal diadem," in His hand: so <reference osisRef="Isa.62.3">Is 62:3</reference>. He is their Possessor and Upholder.<div eID="gen41278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41279" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">out of ... mouth went--</hi>Greek, "going forth"; not wielded in the hand. His Word is omnipotent in executing His will in punishing sinners. It is the sword of His Spirit. Reproof and punishment, rather than its converting winning power, is the prominent point. Still, as He encourages the churches, as well as threatens, the former quality of the Word is not excluded. Its two edges (back and front) may allude to its double efficacy, condemning some, converting others. Tertullian [Epistle against Judaizers], takes them of the Old and the New Testaments. Richard of St. Victor, "the Old Testament cutting externally our carnal, the New Testament internally, our spiritual sins."<div eID="gen41279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41280" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sword--</hi>Greek, "romphaia," the Thracian long and heavy broad sword: six times in Revelation, once only elsewhere in New Testament, namely, <reference osisRef="Luke.2.35">Lu 2:35</reference>.<div eID="gen41280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41281" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sun ... in his strength--</hi>in unclouded power. So shall the righteous shine, reflecting the image of the Sun of righteousness. Trench notices that this description, sublime as a purely mental conception, would be intolerable if we were to give it an outward form. With the Greeks, æsthecial taste was the first consideration, to which all others must give way. With the Hebrews, truth and the full representation ideally of the religious reality were the paramount consideration, that representation being designed not to be outwardly embodied, but to remain a purely mental conception. This exalting of the essence above the form marks their deeper religious earnestness. <div eID="gen41281" type="x-p"/>
entries.ae3b3522f38be1f49c30a7b014d9f7c90ec955ae: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19063"/><div sID="gen41282" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19063"/>17. So fallen is man that God's manifestation of His glorious presence overwhelms him.<div eID="gen41282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41283" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">laid his right hand upon me--</hi>So the same Lord Jesus did at the Transfiguration to the three prostrate disciples, of whom John was one, saying, Be not afraid. The "touch" of His hand, as of old, imparted strength.<div eID="gen41283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41284" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto me--</hi>omitted in the oldest manuscripts.<div eID="gen41284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41285" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the first ... the last--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.41.4">Is 41:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.44.6">44:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.48.12">48:12</reference>). From eternity, and enduring to eternity: "the First by creation, the Last by retribution: the First, because before Me there was no God formed; the Last, because after Me there shall be no other: the First, because from Me are all things; the Last, because to Me all things return" [Richard of St. Victor]. <div eID="gen41285" type="x-p"/>
entries.78f14dfbbc72b744479eea1348c2411f703311f4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19064"/><div sID="gen41286" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19064"/>18. Translate as Greek, "And THE Living One": connected with last sentence, <reference osisRef="Rev.1.17">Re 1:17</reference>.<div eID="gen41286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41287" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and was--</hi>Greek, "and (yet) I became."<div eID="gen41287" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41288" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">alive for evermore--</hi>Greek, "living unto the ages of ages": not merely "I live," but I have life, and am the source of it to My people. "To Him belongs absolute being, as contrasted with the relative being of the creature; others may share, He only hath immortality: being in essence, not by mere participation, immortal" [Theodoret in Trench]. One oldest manuscript, with English Version, reads Amen." Two others, and most of the oldest versions and Fathers, omit it. His having passed through death as one of us, and now living in the infinite plenitude of life, reassures His people, since through Him death is the gate of resurrection to eternal life.<div eID="gen41288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41289" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">have ... keys of hell--</hi>Greek, "Hades"; Hebrew, "Sheol." "Hell" in the sense, the place of torment, answers to a different Greek word, namely, Gehenna. I can release from the unseen world of spirits and from DEATH whom I will. The oldest manuscripts read by transposition, "Death and Hades," or Hell." It is death (which came in by sin, robbing man of his immortal birthright, <reference osisRef="Rom.5.12">Ro 5:12</reference>) that peoples Hades, and therefore should stand first in order. Keys are emblems of authority, opening and shutting at will "the gates of Hades" (<reference osisRef="Ps.9.13">Psa 9:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.9.14">14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.38.10">Is 38:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.16.18">Mt 16:18</reference>). <div eID="gen41289" type="x-p"/>
entries.0739c20b14d0c3cada1f4db5acb6ff65de7e2c2e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19065"/><div sID="gen41290" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19065"/>19. The oldest manuscripts read, "Write therefore" (inasmuch as I, "the First and Last," have the keys of death, and vouchsafe to thee this vision for the comfort and warning of the Church).<div eID="gen41290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41291" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">things which are--</hi>"the things which thou hast seen" are those narrated in this chapter (compare <reference osisRef="Rev.1.11">Re 1:11</reference>). "The things which are" imply the present state of things in the churches when John was writing, as represented in the second and third chapters. "The things which shall be hereafter," the things symbolically represented concerning the future history of the fourth through twenty-second chapters. Alford translates, "What things they signify"; but the antithesis of the next clause forbids this, "the things which shall be hereafter," Greek, "which are about to come to pass." The plural (Greek) "are," instead of the usual Greek construction singular, is owing to churches and persons being meant by things" in the clause, "the things which are." <div eID="gen41291" type="x-p"/>
entries.0686c44c836830cda6f01de524bed28025646755: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19066"/><div sID="gen41292" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19066"/><hi type="bold">20. in--</hi>Greek, "upon My right hand."<div eID="gen41292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41293" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the mystery ... candlesticks--</hi>in apposition to, and explaining, "the things which thou hast seen," governed by "Write." Mystery signifies the hidden truth, veiled under this symbol, and now revealed; its correlative is revelation. Stars symbolize lordship (<reference osisRef="Num.24.17">Nu 24:17</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Dan.12.3">Da 12:3</reference>, of faithful teachers; <reference osisRef="Rev.8.10">Re 8:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.12.4">12:4</reference>; Jude 13).<div eID="gen41293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41294" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">angels--</hi>not as Alford, from Origen [Homily 13 on Luke, and Homily 20 on Numbers], the guardian angels of the churches, just as individuals have their guardian angels. For how could heavenly angels be charged with the delinquencies laid here to the charge of these angels? Then, if a human angel be meant (as the Old Testament analogy favors, <reference osisRef="Hag.1.13">Hag 1:13</reference>, "the Lord's Messenger in the Lord's message"; Mal 2:7; 3:1), the bishop, or superintendent pastor, must be the angel. For whereas there were many presbyters in each of the larger churches (as for example, Ephesus, Smyrna, &c.), there was but one angel, whom, moreover, the Chief Shepherd and Bishop of souls holds responsible for the spiritual state of the Church under him. The term angel, designating an office, is, in accordance with the enigmatic symbolism of this book, transferred from the heavenly to the earthly superior ministers of Jehovah; reminding them that, like the heavenly angels above, they below should fulfil God's mission zealously, promptly and efficiently. "Thy will be done on earth, as it is in heaven!" <chapter eID="Rev.1"/>

entries.579ada2165b1460c26cecee703897841139abc0c: <div eID="gen55582" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Preface to the Revelation of St. John the Divine</title> <div sID="gen55583" type="x-p"/> Among the interpreters of the Apocalypse, both in ancient and modern times, we find a vast diversity of opinions, but they may be all reduced to four principal hypotheses, or modes of interpretation: - <div eID="gen55583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55584" type="x-p"/> 1. The Apocalypse contains a prophetical description of the destruction of Jerusalem, of the Jewish war, and the civil wars of the Romans. <div eID="gen55584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55585" type="x-p"/> 2. It contains predictions of the persecutions of the Christians under the heathen emperors of Rome, and of the happy days of the Church under the Christian emperors, from Constantine downwards. <div eID="gen55585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55586" type="x-p"/> 3. It contains prophecies concerning the tyrannical and oppressive conduct of the Roman pontiffs, the true antichrist; and foretells the final destruction of popery. <div eID="gen55586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55587" type="x-p"/> 4. It is a prophetic declaration of the schism and heresies of Martin Luther, those called Reformers, and their successors; and the final destruction of the Protestant religion. <div eID="gen55587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55588" type="x-p"/> The first opinion has been defended by Professor Wetstein, and other learned men on the continent. <div eID="gen55588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55589" type="x-p"/> The second is the opinion of the primitive fathers in general, both Greek and Latin. <div eID="gen55589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55590" type="x-p"/> The third was first broached by the Abb Joachim, who flourished in the thirteenth century, was espoused by most of the Franciscans; and has been and still is the general opinion of the Protestants. <div eID="gen55590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55591" type="x-p"/> The fourth seems to have been invented by popish writers, merely by way of retaliation; and has been illustrated and defended at large by a Mr. Walmsley, (I believe), titular dean of Wells, in a work called the History of the Church, under the feigned name of Signior Pastorini. <div eID="gen55591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55592" type="x-p"/> In this work he endeavors to turn every thing against Luther and the Protestants, which they interpreted of the pope and popery; and attempts to show, from a computation of the Apocalyptical numbers, that the total destruction of Protestantism in the world will take place in 1825! But this is not the first prophecy that has been invented for the sake of an event, the accomplishment of which was earnestly desired; and as a stimulus to excite general attention, and promote united exertion, when the time of the pretended prophecy was fulfilled. But 1825 is past by, and 1832 is come, and the Protestant Church is still in full vigor, while the Romish Church is fast declining. <div eID="gen55592" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55593" type="x-p"/> The full title of the book which I quote is the following: - "The General History of the Christian Church, from her birth to her final triumphant state in Heaven, chiefly deduced from the Apocalypse of St. John the Apostle. By Sig. Pastorini. 'Blessed is he that readeth and heareth the words of this prophecy.' - Apocalypse, <reference osisRef="Rev.1.3">Rev 1:3</reference>. <div eID="gen55593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55594" type="x-p"/> Printed in the year M.DCC.LXXI." 8vo. No place nor printer's name mentioned. <div eID="gen55594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55595" type="x-p"/> The place where he foretells the final destruction of Protestantism is in pp. 249 and 262. <div eID="gen55595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55596" type="x-p"/> The Catholic college of Maynooth, in Ireland, have lately published a new edition of this work! in which the author kindly predicts the approaching overthrow of the whole Protestant system, both in Church and state; and in the meantime gives them, most condescendingly, Abaddon or the devil for their king! <div eID="gen55596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55597" type="x-p"/> Who the writer of the Apocalypse was, learned men are not agreed. This was a question, as well in ancient as in modern times. We have already seen that many have attributed it to the Apostle John; others, to a person called John the presbyter, who they say was an Ephesian, and totally different from John the apostle. And lastly, some have attributed it to Cerinthus, a contemporary of John the apostle. This hypothesis, however, seems utterly unsupportable; as there is no probability that the Christian Church would have so generally received a work which came from the hands of a man at all times reputed a very dangerous heretic; nor can the doctrines it contains ever comport with a Cerinthian creed. <div eID="gen55597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55598" type="x-p"/> Whether it was written by John the apostle, John the presbyter, or some other person, is of little importance if the question of its inspiration be fully established. If written by an apostle it is canonical; and should be received, without hesitation, as a work Divinely inspired. Every apostle acted under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit. John was an apostle, and consequently inspired; therefore, whatever he wrote was written by Divine inspiration. If, therefore, the authenticity of the work be established, i.e., that it was written by John the apostle, all the rest necessarily follow. <div eID="gen55598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55599" type="x-p"/> As I have scarcely any opinion to give concerning this book on which I could wish any of my readers to rely, I shall not enter into any discussion relative to the author, or the meaning of his several visions and prophecies; but for general information refer to Dr. Lardner, Michaelis, and others. <div eID="gen55599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55600" type="x-p"/> Various attempts have been made by learned men to fix the plan of this work; but even in this few agree. I shall produce some of the chief of these: and first, that of Wetstein, which is the most singular of the whole. <div eID="gen55600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55601" type="x-p"/> He supposes the book of the Apocalypse to have been written a considerable time before the destruction of Jerusalem. The events described from the fourth chapter to the end he supposes to refer to the Jewish war, and to the civil commotions which took place in Italy while Otho, Vitellius, and Vespasian were contending for the empire. These contentions and destructive wars occupied the space of about three years and a half, during which Professor Wetstein thinks the principal events took place which are recorded in this book. On these subjects he speaks particularly in his notes, at the end of which he subjoins what he calls his Ανακεφαλαιωσις, or synopsis of the whole work, which I proceed now to lay before the reader. "This prophecy, which predicts the calamities which God should send on the enemies of the Gospel, is divided into two parts. The first is contained in the closed book; the second, in the open book. <div eID="gen55601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55602" type="x-p"/> I. The first concerns the earth and the third part, i.e., Judea and the Jewish nation, <div eID="gen55602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55603" type="x-p"/> II. The second concerns many peoples, and nations, and tongues, and kings, <reference osisRef="Rev.10.11">Rev 10:11</reference>, i.e., the Roman empire. <div eID="gen55603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55604" type="x-p"/> 1. The book written within and without, and sealed with seven seals, <reference osisRef="Rev.5.1">Rev 5:1</reference>, is the bill of divorce sent from God to the Jewish nation. <div eID="gen55604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55605" type="x-p"/> 2. The crowned conqueror on the white horse armed with a bow, <reference osisRef="Rev.6.2">Rev 6:2</reference>, is Artabanus, king of the Parthians, who slaughtered multitudes of the Jews in Babylon. <div eID="gen55605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55606" type="x-p"/> 3. The red horse, <reference osisRef="Rev.6.4">Rev 6:4</reference>. The Sicarii and robbers in Judea, in the time of the Proconsuls Felix and Festus. <div eID="gen55606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55607" type="x-p"/> 4. The black horse, <reference osisRef="Rev.6.5">Rev 6:5</reference>. The famine under Claudius. <div eID="gen55607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55608" type="x-p"/> 5. The pale horse, <reference osisRef="Rev.6.8">Rev 6:8</reference>. The plague which followed the robberies and the famine. <div eID="gen55608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55609" type="x-p"/> 6. The souls of those who were slain, <reference osisRef="Rev.6.9">Rev 6:9</reference>. The Christians in Judea, who were persecuted, and were now about to be avenged. <div eID="gen55609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55610" type="x-p"/> 7. The great earthquake, <reference osisRef="Rev.6.12">Rev 6:12</reference>. The commotions which preceded the Jewish rebellion. <div eID="gen55610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55611" type="x-p"/> 8. The servants of God from every tribe, sealed in their foreheads, <reference osisRef="Rev.7.3">Rev 7:3</reference>. The Christians taken under the protection of God, and warned by the prophets to flee immediately from the land. <div eID="gen55611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55612" type="x-p"/> 9. The silence for half an hour, <reference osisRef="Rev.8.1">Rev 8:1</reference>. The short truce granted at the solicitation of King Agrippa. Then follows the rebellion itself. <div eID="gen55612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55613" type="x-p"/> 1. The trees are burnt, <reference osisRef="Rev.8.7">Rev 8:7</reference>. The fields and villages, and unfortified places of Judea, which first felt the bad effects of the sedition. <div eID="gen55613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55614" type="x-p"/> 2. The burning mountain cast into the sea which in consequence became blood, <reference osisRef="Rev.8.8">Rev 8:8</reference>; and, <div eID="gen55614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55615" type="x-p"/> 3. The burning star falling into the rivers, and making the waters bitter, <reference osisRef="Rev.8.10">Rev 8:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.8.11">Rev 8:11</reference>. The slaughter of the Jews at Caesarea and Scythopolis. <div eID="gen55615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55616" type="x-p"/> 4. The eclipsing of the sun, moon, and stars, <reference osisRef="Rev.8.12">Rev 8:12</reference>. Test., vol. ii. p. 889. <div eID="gen55651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55652" type="x-p"/> Those who consider the Apocalypse as a prophecy and scenical exhibition of what shall happen to the Christian Church to the end of the world, lay this down as a proposition, which comprises the subject of the whole book: The contest of Christ with his enemies; and his final victory and triumph over them. See <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.25">1Cor 15:25</reference>; Matthew 24:1-51; Mark 13:1-37; Luke 21:5-38. But what is but briefly hinted in the above scriptures, is detailed at large in the Apocalypse, and represented by various images nearly in the following order: - <div eID="gen55652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55653" type="x-p"/> 1. The decrees of the Divine providence, concerning what is to come, are declared to John. <div eID="gen55653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55654" type="x-p"/> 2. The manner in which these decrees shall be executed is painted in the most vivid colors. <div eID="gen55654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55655" type="x-p"/> 3. Then follow thanksgivings to God, the ruler and governor of all things, for these manifestations of his power, wisdom and goodness. <div eID="gen55655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55656" type="x-p"/> After the exordium, and the seven epistles to the seven Churches of Asia Minor, to whose angels or bishops the book seems to be dedicated, (Revelation 1:1-3:22), the scene of the visions is opened in heaven, full of majesty; and John receives a promise of a revelation relative to the future state of the Church, Revelation 4:1-5:14. <div eID="gen55656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55657" type="x-p"/> The enemies of the Church of Christ which the Christians had then most to fear were the Jews, the heathens, and the false teachers. All these are overcome by Christ, and over them he triumphs gloriously. First of all, punishments are threatened to the enemies of the kingdom of Christ, and the preservation of his own followers in their greatest trials determined; and these determinations are accompanied with the praises and thanksgivings of all the heavenly inhabitants, and of all good men, Revelation 6:1-10:11. <div eID="gen55657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55658" type="x-p"/> The transactions of the Christian religion are next recorded, Revelation 11:1-14:5. The Christians are persecuted: - <div eID="gen55658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55659" type="x-p"/> 1. By the Jews; but they were not only preserved, but they increase and prosper. <div eID="gen55659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55660" type="x-p"/> 2. By the heathens; but in vain do these strive to overthrow the kingdom of Christ, which is no longer confined within the limits of Judea, but spreads among the Gentiles, and diffuses itself over the whole Roman empire, destroying idolatry, and rooting out superstition, in every quarter, Revelation 12:1-13:10. <div eID="gen55660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55661" type="x-p"/> 3. False teachers and impostors of various kinds, under the name of Christians, but enemies of the cross of Christ, more intent on promoting the interests of idolatry or false worship than the cause of true religion, <reference osisRef="Rev.13.11-Rev.13.18">Rev 13:11-18</reference>, exert their influence to corrupt and destroy the Church; but, notwithstanding, Christianity becomes more extended, and true believers more confirmed in their holy faith, <reference osisRef="Rev.14.1-Rev.14.5">Rev 14:1-5</reference>. Then new punishments are decreed against the enemies of Christ, both Jews and heathens: the calamities coming upon the Jewish nation before its final overthrow are pointed out, Revelation 14:1-15:8. Next follows a prediction of the calamities which shall take place during the Jewish war; and the civil wars of the Romans during the contentions of Otho and Vitellius, Revelation 16:1-16, who are to suffer most grievous punishments for their cruelties against the Christians, Revelation 17:1-18. The Jewish state being now finally overthrown, Revelation 18:1-24, the heavenly inhabitants give praise to God for his justice and goodness; Christ is congratulated for his victory over his enemies, and the more extensive progress of his religion, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.1-Rev.19.10">Rev 19:1-10</reference>. <div eID="gen55661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55662" type="x-p"/> Opposition is, however, not yet totally ended: idolatry again lifts up its head, and new errors are propagated; but over these also Christ shows himself to be conqueror, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.11-Rev.19.21">Rev 19:11-21</reference>. Finally, Satan, who had long reigned by the worship of false gods, errors, superstitions, and wickedness, is deprived of all power and influence; and the concerns of Christianity go on gloriously, <reference osisRef="Rev.20.1-Rev.20.6">Rev 20:1-6</reference>. But towards the end of the world new enemies arise, and threaten destruction to the followers of Christ; but in vain is their rage, God appears in behalf of his servants, and inflicts the most grievous punishments upon their adversaries, <reference osisRef="Rev.20.6-Rev.20.10">Rev 20:6-10</reference>. The last judgment ensues, <reference osisRef="Rev.20.11-Rev.20.15">Rev 20:11-15</reference>, all the wicked are punished, and the enemies of the truth are chained, so as to be able to injure the godly no more; the genuine Christians, who had persevered unto death, are brought to eternal glory; and, freed from all adversities, spend a life that shall never end, in blessedness that knows no bounds, Revelation 21:1-22:21. See Rosenmuller. <div eID="gen55662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55663" type="x-p"/> Eichhorn takes a different view of the plan of this book; though in substance not differing much from that above. According to this writer the whole is represented in the form of a drama, the parts of which are the following: <div eID="gen55663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55664" type="x-p"/> I. The title, <reference osisRef="Rev.1.1-Rev.1.3">Rev 1:1-3</reference>. <div eID="gen55664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55665" type="x-p"/> II. The prologue, Revelation 1:4-3:22; in which it is stated that the argument of the drama refers to the Christians; epistles being sent to the Churches, which, in the symbolic style, are represented by the number seven. <div eID="gen55665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55666" type="x-p"/> Next follows the drama itself, the parts of which are: - <div eID="gen55666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55667" type="x-p"/> The prolusio, or prelude, Revelation 4:1-8:5; in which the scenery is prepared and adorned. <div eID="gen55667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55668" type="x-p"/> Act the first, Revelation 8:6-12:17. Jerusalem is taken, and Judaism vanquished by Christianity. <div eID="gen55668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55669" type="x-p"/> Act the second, Revelation 13:1-20:10. Rome is conquered, and heathenism destroyed by the Christian religion. <div eID="gen55669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55670" type="x-p"/> Act the third, Revelation 20:11-22:5. The New Jerusalem descends from heaven; or the happiness of the life to come, and which is to endure for ever, is particularly described, <reference osisRef="Rev.22.6-Rev.22.11">Rev 22:6-11</reference>. Taken in this sense, Eichhorn supposes the work to be most exquisitely finished, and its author to have had a truly poetic mind, polished by the highest cultivation; to have been accurately acquainted with the history of all times and nations, and to have enriched himself with their choicest spoils. <div eID="gen55670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55671" type="x-p"/> My readers will naturally expect that I should either give a decided preference to some one of the opinions stated above, or produce one of my own; I can do neither, nor can I pretend to explain the book: I do not understand it; and in the things which concern so sublime and awful a subject, I dare not, as my predecessors, indulge in conjectures. I have read elaborate works on the subject, and each seemed right till another was examined. I am satisfied that no certain mode of interpreting the prophecies of this book has yet been found out, and I will not add another monument to the littleness or folly of the human mind by endeavoring to strike out a new course. I repeat it, I do not understand the book; and I am satisfied that not one who has written on the subject knows any thing more of it than myself. I should, perhaps, except J. E. Clarke, who has written on the number of the beast. His interpretation amounts nearly to demonstration; but that is but a small part of the difficulties of the Apocalypse: that interpretation, as the most probable ever yet offered to the public, shall be inserted in its proper place; as also his illustration of the xiith, xiiith, and xviith chapters. As to other matters, I must leave them to God, or to those events which shall point out the prophecy; and then, and probably not till then, will the sense of these visions be explained. <div eID="gen55671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55672" type="x-p"/> A conjecture concerning the design of the book may be safely indulged; thus then it has struck me, that the book of the Apocalypse may be considered as a Prophet continued in the Church of God, uttering predictions relative to all times, which have their successive fulfillment as ages roll on; and thus it stands in the Christian Church in the place of the Succession of Prophets in the Jewish Church; and by this especial economy Prophecy is Still Continued, is Always Speaking; and yet a succession of prophets rendered unnecessary. If this be so, we cannot too much admire the wisdom of the contrivance which still continues the voice and testimony of prophecy, by means of a very short book, without the assistance of any extraordinary messenger, or any succession of such messengers, whose testimony would at all times be liable to suspicion, and be the subject of infidel and malevolent criticism, howsoever unexceptionable to ingenuous minds the credentials of such might appear. <div eID="gen55672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55673" type="x-p"/> On this ground it is reasonable to suppose that several prophecies contained in this book have been already fulfilled, and that therefore it is the business of the commentator to point such out. It may be so; but as it is impossible for me to prove that my conjecture is right, I dare not enter into proceedings upon it, and must refer to Bishop Newton, and such writers as have made this their particular study. <div eID="gen55673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55674" type="x-p"/> After having lived in one of the most eventful eras of the world; after having seen a number of able pens employed in the illustration of this and other prophecies; after having carefully attended to those facts which were supposed to be the incontestable proofs of the fulfillment of such and such visions, seals, trumpets, thunders, and vials of the Apocalypse; after seeing the issue of that most terrible struggle which the French nation, the French republic, the French consulate, and the French empire, have made to regain and preserve their liberties, which, like arguing in a circle, have terminated where they began, without one political or religious advantage to them or to mankind; and after viewing how the prophecies of this book were supposed to apply almost exclusively to these events, the writers and explainers of these prophecies keeping pace in their publications with the rapid succession of military operations, and confidently promising the most glorious issue, in the final destruction of superstition, despotism, arbitrary power, and tyranny of all kinds, nothing of which has been realized; I say, viewing all these things, I feel myself at perfect liberty to state that, to my apprehension, all these prophecies have been misapplied and misapprehended; and that the Key to them is not yet intrusted to the sons of men. My readers will therefore excuse me from any exposure of my ignorance or folly by attempting to do what many, with much more wisdom and learning, have attempted, and what every man to the present day has failed in, who has preceded me in expositions of this book. I have no other mountain to heap on those already piled up; and if I had, I have not strength to lift it: those who have courage may again make the trial; already we have had a sufficiency of vain efforts. <div eID="gen55674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55675" type="x-p"/> Ter sunt conati imponere Pelio Ossam <div eID="gen55675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55676" type="x-p"/> Scilicet, atque Ossae frondosum involvere Olympum: <div eID="gen55676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55677" type="x-p"/> Ter Pater extructos disjecit fulmine montes. <div eID="gen55677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55678" type="x-p"/> Virg., G. i. 281. <div eID="gen55678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55679" type="x-p"/> With mountains piled on mountains thrice they strove <div eID="gen55679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55680" type="x-p"/> To scale the steepy battlements of Jove; <div eID="gen55680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55681" type="x-p"/> And thrice his lightning and red thunder play'd, <div eID="gen55681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55682" type="x-p"/> And their demolish'd works in ruin laid. <div eID="gen55682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55683" type="x-p"/> Dryden <div eID="gen55683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55684" type="x-p"/> I had resolved, for a considerable time, not to meddle with this book, because I foresaw that I could produce nothing satisfactory on it: but when I reflected that the literal sense and phraseology might be made much plainer by the addition of philological and critical notes; and that, as the diction appeared in many places to be purely rabbinical, (a circumstance to which few of its expositors have attended), it might be rendered plainer by examples from the ancient Jewish writers; and that several parts of it spoke directly of the work of God in the soul of man, and of the conflicts and consolations of the followers of Christ, particularly in the beginning of the book, I changed my resolution, and have added short notes, principally philological, where I thought I understood the meaning. <div eID="gen55684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55685" type="x-p"/> I had once thought of giving a catalogue of the writers and commentators on this book, and had begun a collection of this kind; but the question of Cui bono? What good end is this likely to serve? not meeting with a satisfactory answer in my own mind, caused me to throw this collection aside. I shall notice two only. <div eID="gen55685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55686" type="x-p"/> 1. The curious and learned work entitled, "A plaine Discovery of the whole Revelation of St. John," written by Sir John Napier, inventor of the logarithms, I have particularly described in the general preface to the Holy Scriptures, prefixed to the Book of Genesis, to which the reader is requested to refer. <div eID="gen55686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55687" type="x-p"/> 2. Another work, not less singular, and very rare, entitled, "The Image of both Churches, after the most wonderful and heavenly Revelation of Sainct John the Evangelist, containing a very fruitfull exposition or paraphrase upon the same: wherein it is conferred with the other scriptures, and most auctorised histories Compyled by John Bale, an exyle also in thys lyfe for the faithful testimony of Jesu." Printed at London by Thomas East, 18mo., without date. <div eID="gen55687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55688" type="x-p"/> The author was at first a Carmelite, but was afterwards converted to the Protestant religion. He has turned the whole of the Apocalypse against the Romish Church; and it is truly astonishing to see with what address he directs every image, metaphor, and description, contained in this book, against the corruptions of this Church. He was made bishop of Ossory, in Ireland; but was so persecuted by the papists that he narrowly escaped with his life, five of his domestics being murdered by them. On the accession of Mary he was obliged to take refuge in the Low Countries, where it appears he compiled this work. As he was bred up a papist, and was also a priest, he possessed many advantages in attacking the strongest holds of his adversaries. He knew all their secrets, and he uncovered the whole; he was acquainted with all their rites, ceremonies, and superstitions, and finds all distinctly marked in the Apocalypse, which he believes was written to point out the abominations, and to foretell the final destruction of this corrupt and intolerant Church. I shall make a few references to his work in the course of the following notes. In <reference osisRef="Rev.17.1">Rev 17:1</reference>, the author shows his opinion, and speaks something of himself: Come hither, I will show thee the judgment of the great whore, etc. "Come hither, friende John, I will show thee in secretnesse the tirrible judgement of the great whore, or counterfaite Church of hypocrites. Needs must this whore be Rome, for that she is the great citie which reigneth over the kings of the earth. Evident it is both by Scriptures and Cronicles that in John's dayes Rome had dominion over all the whole world: and being infected with the abominations of all landes, rightly is shee called Babylon. or Citie of Confusion. And like as in the Scriptures ofte tymes under the name of Jerusalem is ment the whole kingdom of Juda, so under the name of Rome here may be understanded the unyversall worlde, with all their abominations and divilleshnesses, their idolatryes, witchcraftes, sectes, superstitions, papacyes, priesthoodes, relygions, shavings, anointings, blessings, sensings, processions, and the divil of all such beggeryes. For all the people since Christes assencion, hath this Rome infected with hir pestilent poisons gathered from all idolatrous nations, such time as she held over them the monarchial suppremit. At the wryting of this prophecy felt John of their cruiltie, being exiled into Pathmos for the faithfull testimony of Jesu. And so did I, poore creature, with my poore wife and children, at the gatheringe of this present commentary, flying into Germanye for the same," etc. <div eID="gen55688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55689" type="x-p"/> Shall I have the reader's pardon if I say that it is my firm opinion that the expositions of this book have done great disservice to religion: almost every commentator has become a prophet; for as soon as he began to explain he began also to prophesy. And what has been the issue? Disappointment laughed at hope's career, and superficial thinkers have been led to despise and reject prophecy itself. I shall sum up all that I wish to say farther in the words of Graserus: Mihi tota Apocalypsis valde obscura videtur; et talis, cujus explicatio citra periculum vix queat tentari. Fateor me hactenus in nullius Scripti Biblici lectione minus vroficere, quam in hoc obscurissimo Vaticinio. <div eID="gen55689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55690" type="x-p"/> The preface to this book, and the promise to them who read it, <reference osisRef="Rev.1.1-Rev.1.3">Rev 1:1-3</reference>. John's address to the seven Churches of Asia, whose high calling he particularly mentions; and shows the speedy coming of Christ, <reference osisRef="Rev.1.4-Rev.1.8">Rev 1:4-8</reference>. Mentions his exile to Patmos, and the appearance of the Lord Jesus to him, <reference osisRef="Rev.1.9-Rev.1.11">Rev 1:9-11</reference>. Of whom he gives a most glorious description, <reference osisRef="Rev.1.12-Rev.1.18">Rev 1:12-18</reference>. The command to write what he saw, and the explanation of the seven stars and seven golden candlesticks, <reference osisRef="Rev.1.19">Rev 1:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.1.20">Rev 1:20</reference>. <div eID="gen55690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55691" type="x-p"/> The Revelation of St. John the divine. To this book the inscriptions are various. " - The Revelation. - The Revelation of John. - Of John the divine. - Of John the divine and evangelist. - The Revelation of John the apostle and evangelist. - The Revelation of the holy and glorious apostle and evangelist, the beloved virgin John the divine, which he saw in the island of Patmos. - The Revelation of Jesus Christ, given to John the divine." <div eID="gen55691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55692" type="x-p"/> These several inscriptions are worthy of little regard; the first verse contains the title of the book. <div eID="gen55692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55693" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen55693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55694" type="x-p"/> The Revelation of Jesus Christ - The word Αποκαλυψις, from which we have our word Apocalypse, signifies literally, a revelation, or discovery of what was concealed or hidden. It is here said that this revelation, or discovery of hidden things, was given by God to Jesus Christ; that Christ gave it to his angel; that this angel showed it to John; and that John sent it to the Churches. Thus we find it came from God to Christ, from Christ to the angel, from the angel to John, and from John to the Church. It is properly, therefore, the Revelation of God, sent by these various agents to his servants at large; and this is the proper title of the book. <div eID="gen55694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55695" type="x-p"/> Things which must shortly come to pass - On the mode of interpretation devised by Wetstein, this is plain; for if the book were written before the destruction of Jerusalem, and the prophecies in it relate to that destruction, and the civil wars among the Romans, which lasted but three or four years, then it might be said the Revelation is of things which must shortly come to pass. But if we consider the book as referring to the state of the Church in all ages, the words here, and those in <reference osisRef="Rev.1.3">Rev 1:3</reference>, must be understood of the commencement of the events predicted; as if he had said: In a short time the train of these visions will be put in motion: - - et incipient magni procedere menses. "And those times, pregnant with the most stupendous events, will begin to roll on."
entries.3723f6a4625b42e18c34c0b4158a08a1471d82d7: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen55695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55696" type="x-p"/> Who bare record of the word of God - Is there a reference here to the first chapter of John's gospel, In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, etc.? Of this Word John did bear record. Or, does the writer mean the fidelity with which he noted and related the word - doctrines or prophecies, which he received at this time by revelation from God? This seems more consistent with the latter part of the verse.
