Compare Rev 2:1,8,12,18; see also similar language in regard to the church in Corinth, 1Cor 1:2; in Antioch, Acts 13:1; at Laodicea, Col 4:16; and at Ephesus, Acts 20:28.

(d) There is no evidence, as Episcopalians must suppose, that a successor to John had been appointed at Ephesus, if, as they suppose, he was "bishop" of Ephesus; and there is no probability that they would so soon after his banishment show him such a want of respect as to regard the see as vacant, and appoint a successor.

(e) There is no improbability in supposing that there was a single church in each of these cities--as at Antioch, Corinth, Rome.

(f) If John was a prelatical "bishop," it is probable that he was "bishop" of the whole group of churches embracing the seven: yet here, if the word "angel" means "bishop," we have no less than seven such bishops immediately appointed to succeed him. And

(g) the supposition that this refers to prelatical bishops is so forced and unnatural that many Episcopalians are compelled to abandon it. Thus Stillingfleet, than whom an abler man, or one whose praise is higher in episcopal churches, as an advocate of prelacy, is not to be found, says of these angels: "If many things in the epistles be directed to the angels, but yet so as to concern the whole body, then, of necessity, the angel must be taken as a representative of the whole body; and then why may not the angel be taken by way of representation of the body itself, either of the whole church, or, which is far more probable, of the concessors, or order of presbyters in this church?"

(4.) If the word does not mean literally an angel; if it does not refer to messengers sent to John in Patmos by the churches; and if it does not refer to a prelatical bishop, then it follows that it must refer to some one who presided over the church as its pastor, and through whom a message might be properly sent to the church. Thus understood, the pastor or "angel" would be regarded as the representative of the church; that is, as delegated by the church to manage its affairs, and as the authorized person to whom communications should be made in matters pertaining to it-- as pastors are now. A few considerations will further confirm this interpretation, and throw additional light on the meaning of the word.

(a) The word angel is employed in the Old Testament to denote a prophet; that is, a minister of religion as sent by God to communicate his will. Thus in Haggai (Hag 1:13) it is said, "Then spoke Haggai, the Lord's messenger, [Heb. angel, --Septuagint αγγελοςκυριου] in the Lord's message unto the people," etc.

(b) It is applied to a priest, as one sent by God to execute the functions of that office, or to act in the name of the Lord. Mal 2:7, "For the priest's lips should keep knowledge, for he is the messenger of the Lord of hosts"----that is, "angel of the Lord of hosts."

(c) The name prophet is often given in the New Testament to the ministers of religion, as being appointed by God to proclaim or communicate his will to his people, and as occupying a place resembling, in some respects, that of the prophets in the Old Testament.

(d) There was no reason why the word might not be thus employed to designate a pastor of a Christian church, as well as to designate a prophet or a priest under the Old Testament dispensation.

(e) The supposition that a pastor of a church is intended will meet all the circumstances of the case: for,

(1) it is an appropriate appellation;

(2) there is no reason to suppose that there was more than one church in each of the cities referred to;

(3) it is a term which would designate the respect in which the office was held;

(4) it would impress upon those to whom it was applied a solemn sense of their responsibility. Further, it would be more appropriately applied to a pastor of a single church than to a prelatical bishop; to the tender, intimate, and endearing relation sustained by a pastor to his people, to the blending of sympathy, interest, and affection, where he is with them continually, meets them frequently in the sanctuary, administers to them the bread of life, goes into their abodes when they are afflicted, and attends their kindred to the grave, than to the union subsisting between the people of an extended diocese and a prelate--the formal, unfrequent, and, in many instances, stately and pompous visitations of a diocesan bishop--to the unsympathising relation between him and a people scattered in many churches, who are visited at distant intervals by one claiming a "superiority in ministerial rights and powers," and who must be a stranger to the ten thousand ties of endearment which bind the hearts of a pastor and people together. The conclusion, then, to which we have come is, that the "angel of the church" was the pastor, or the presiding presbyter in the church; the minister who had the pastoral charge of it, and who was therefore a proper representative of it. He was a man who, in some respects, performed the functions which the angels of God do; that is, who was appointed to execute his will, to communicate his message, and to convey important intimations of his purposes to his people. To no one could the communications in this book, intended for the churches, be more properly entrusted than to such an one; for to no one now would a communication be more properly entrusted than to a pastor.

Such is the sublime vision under which this book opens; such the solemn commission which the penman of the book received. No more appropriate introduction to what is contained in the book could be imagined; no more appropriate circumstances for making such a sublime revelation could have existed. To the most beloved of the apostles--now the only surviving one of the number; to him who had been a faithful labourer for a period not far from sixty years after the death of the Lord Jesus, who had been the bosom friend of the Saviour when in the flesh, who had seen him in the mount of transfiguration, who had seen him die, and who had seen him ascend into heaven; to him who had lived while the church was founded, and while it had spread into all lands; and to him who was now suffering persecution on account of the Saviour and his cause, it was appropriate that such communications should be made. In a lonely island; far away from the abodes of men; surrounded by the ocean, and amid barren rocks; on the day consecrated to the purposes of sacred repose and the holy duties of religion--the day observed in commemoration of the resurrection of his Lord, it was most fit that the Redeemer should appear to the "beloved disciple" in the last Revelation which he was ever to make to mankind. No more appropriate time or circumstance could be conceived for disclosing, by a series of sublime visions, what would occur in future times; for sketching out the history of the church to the consummation of all things.

                     </ns0:gap>es<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ser <ns0:hi>Asia.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>; unto Ephesus <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Ephesus</ns0:hi> was the most famous where <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> preached, <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 19.10. &c. and stayed three years, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 20.31. It was a noble City in that part of <ns0:hi>Greece,</ns0:hi> which was called <ns0:hi>Ionia.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, and unto Smyrna <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Smyrna</ns0:hi> was a Sea-port City in the same Country.</ns0:note>, and unto Pergamos <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Perga<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mos</ns0:hi> was a City of <ns0:hi>Troas,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Phrygia.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, and unto Thya<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tira <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Thyatira</ns0:hi> was a City in <ns0:hi>Lydia,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Mysia.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, and unto Sardis <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Sardis</ns0:hi> also was a City in <ns0:hi>Lydia,</ns0:hi> near the Mountain <ns0:hi>Timolus.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, and unto Philadelphia <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Philadelphia</ns0:hi> was a City in <ns0:hi>Lydia,</ns0:hi> next <ns0:hi>Mysia.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, and unto Laodicea <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Laodicea</ns0:hi> was a City in <ns0:hi>Asia</ns0:hi> near the River <ns0:hi>Lycus.</ns0:hi> In all these Cities there were Congregations of Christians formed into Churches, to whom God here ordereth St. <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> to send these Visions, when he had wrote them in a Book. Our Countryman, Mr. <ns0:hi>Bright<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="3 letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•••</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>
                     </ns0:hi> asks<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Where <ns0:hi>Rome</ns0:hi> was all this while? and how it came to pass God directed not these Mysteries to be sent, and kept in their <ns0:hi>Archieves,</ns0:hi> especially if (as the <ns0:hi>Papists</ns0:hi> say) the <ns0:hi>Bishop</ns0:hi> there be Christ's successive <ns0:hi>Vicar</ns0:hi>? and considering too, how great Friends <ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> were wont to be? But the fore-mentioned Author tart<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly replies to his own Question, That that Church, it seems, could never err, and therefore needed not any Correptory, or monitory Epistle.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 And I turned to see the voice that spake with me <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">That is, to see <ns0:hi>the <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>erson,</ns0:hi> whose Voice I heard speak<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing to me; or else by <ns0:hi>seeing,</ns0:hi> is meant <ns0:hi>Vnderstanding</ns0:hi>; (but that he might have done without turning) he therefore turned, hoping to see the Person that spake.</ns0:note>. And being turned, I saw seven golden candlesticks <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">By these seven Candlesticks which he saw, are meant the seven Churches; so we find it infallibly expounded, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 20. we shall find in this <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> Allusio<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>s to the <ns0:hi>Iewish Temple.</ns0:hi> Here they begin? In the Jewish <ns0:hi>Tabernacle</ns0:hi> there was one <ns0:hi>Golden-Candle<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stick,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>seven Lamps,</ns0:hi> to give <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> against it? so <ns0:hi>Num.</ns0:hi> 8.2. <ns0:hi>Zech.</ns0:hi> 4.2. <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> here seeth seven. God had but one Church of the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> but many amongst the Gentiles. This Notion or Comparison of <ns0:hi>Churches</ns0:hi> to <ns0:hi>Golden-Candlesticks,</ns0:hi> both shew<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth us the Nature, and Office of the Churches of Christ, they do not give Light of themselves, only hold Lights; and it is their Duty to keep in them the pure Word of God, which is a Light to our Feet, and a godly Ministry; and it also lets us know, that they ought to keep themselves pure (as beaten Gold) from all Corruption, as to Doctrine, and their Members from all scandalous Conversation.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:601" />13 And in the midst of the seven candlesticks <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">That is, of the Churches, resembled by the Golden-Candlesticks.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note place="margin">Ezek. 1.26. Dan. 7.13. Chap. 14.14.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:hi>one</ns0:hi> like unto the Son of man <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>One</ns0:hi> like to the Son of Man. We say, no like is the same; but Christ who was the <ns0:hi>Son of Man,</ns0:hi> and who ordinarily calls himself so throughout the Gospel, is undoubtedly here meant, as appeareth by <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 17, 18. which Description can agree to him alone. He is said to have come in the <ns0:hi>likeness of sinful Flesh,</ns0:hi> tho he came in true human Flesh; and <ns0:hi>Phil.</ns0:hi> 2.8. <ns0:hi>He was made in the like<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness of Men. Iohn</ns0:hi> saw one who appeared to him, as a Man, in the midst of seven Golden Candlesticks, which was Christ in the midst of his Churches; placed in the midst, partly to let us know his Observation of them all, and partly to let us know his being at hand to them all, to help, protect, and defend them.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Dan. 10.5, 6.</ns0:note> clothed with a garment down to the foot <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, the word signifieth a long Gar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment reaching to the Feet, whether of <ns0:hi>Linen</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Woollen,</ns0:hi> or what other material is not expressed; so as it seemeth to me hard to determine, Whether it was to signifie his <ns0:hi>Priestly,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Kingly office,</ns0:hi> or neither. It is an Habit of Gravity</ns0:note>, and <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Chap. 15.6.</ns0:note> gi<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                     <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                  </ns0:gap>t about the paps with a golden girdle <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Nor dare I determine the Significancy of the Golden Girdle about his Loins. It was an Habit like that in <ns0:hi>Daniel</ns0:hi>'s Vision, <ns0:hi>Dan.</ns0:hi> 10.5. They were both <ns0:hi>Symbols</ns0:hi> of <ns0:hi>Majesty, Authority,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Dig<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nity,</ns0:hi> and the Appearance agreed very well to him, who was both an High-Priest, and a King.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 His head and <ns0:hi>his</ns0:hi> hairs <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> white like wooll, as white as snow <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Whiteness signifies Purity; whiteness of Hair signifies Old Age ordinarily, which commonly is attended with more Prudence, as having most Experience: hence this Appea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rance of Christ may both denote his Purity, and Wisdom, and that he is the <ns0:hi>Ancient of Days</ns0:hi>; See <ns0:hi>Dan.</ns0:hi> 7.9, 13, 22. tho there the term of <ns0:hi>Ancient of Days</ns0:hi> belongs to God the Father, yet it also agreeth to Christ, who is equal with the Father, as to his Divine Nature.</ns0:note>; and his eyes <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> as a flame of fire <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Such an Appearance is applied to God, <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 1.27. <ns0:hi>Dan.</ns0:hi> 10.6. and to Christ, <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 19.12. to denote either Christ's <ns0:hi>Knowledge, Wisdom,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Omniscience</ns0:hi>; or his Grace in purifying Souls, as Fire doth Metals; or his Wrath and Anger against his Enemies.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 And his feet like unto fine brass <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">There are nice Disquisitions what this <ns0:hi>Chalcolibanum</ns0:hi> (which we translate, fine Brass) was: <ns0:hi>vid. Poli Synopsin.</ns0:hi> I understand not of what Profit the Determination will be to us. By the Feet of <ns0:hi>Christ</ns0:hi> (probably) are signified his Ways, Counsels, and Methods in ordering, and govern<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing his Church, which are compared to fine Brass, for the Beauty and Glory of them, and for their Firmitude, Strength, and Steadiness.</ns0:note>, as if they burned in a furnace <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">They appeared like Brass filled with Fire, as if it were burning, and red-hot in a Furnace.</ns0:note>; and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 14.2.</ns0:note> his voice as the sound of many waters <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Loud, and terrible, like the noise of the Sea dashing upon a Rock, or the Shore.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">16 And he had in his right hand seven stars <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">The Right Hand is the Hand of <ns0:hi>Power,</ns0:hi> Psal. 21.8. and 44.3. and of <ns0:hi>Favour,</ns0:hi> Psal. 110.1. and of <ns0:hi>Honour</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Digni<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ty.</ns0:hi> The <ns0:hi>seven Stars</ns0:hi> are expounded, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 20. to be the Mini<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sters of the Gospel, his Messengers to his Churches, who having in all times been most exposed to the Malice and Rage of Enemies. Christ is said to hold them in his Right-Hand, as to signifie the <ns0:hi>Dignity</ns0:hi> he hath put upon them, and the <ns0:hi>Favour</ns0:hi> he hath shewed them; so also to shew his Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />solution to protect them, according to his Promise, <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 28.20.</ns0:note>, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Isa. 49.2. Chap. 2.16. & 19.<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>15, 21.</ns0:note> out of his mouth went a sharp two-edged sword <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Either his Gospel and Word compared to a two-edged Sword, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 4.12. or a Sword of Justice, which he will use till he hath perfectly overcome, and vanquished his Enemies.</ns0:note>, and his countenance <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> as the sun shining in his strength <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">That is, was very glorious, so as the Apostle was not able to behold him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 And when I saw him, I fell at his feet as dead <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Astonished at the Majesty and Glory of the Appea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rance; see <ns0:hi>Iosh.</ns0:hi> 5.14. <ns0:hi>Dan.</ns0:hi> 8.17, 18. <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 17.6. <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 9.4.</ns0:note>, And he <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Dan. 10.10.</ns0:note> laid his right hand up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on me, saying unto me, Fear not <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">To comfort me, and let me know, that I had no reason to be afraid, he would do me no harm.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Isa. 41.4. & 44.6. Chap. 2.8.</ns0:note> I am the first, and the last <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">See <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 8, 11.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">18 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 6.9.</ns0:note> I <ns0:hi>am</ns0:hi> he that liveth, and was dead; and behold, I am alive for evermore <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">The living God, who had Life in my self, and gave life to the World, but assumed the Human Nature, and was made Man, and in that Nature died, but I rose again from thedead, and shall die no more, but ever live to make In<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tercession for my People.</ns0:note>, Amen <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">This is a great Truth.</ns0:note>; and <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Psal. 68.20. Chap. 20.1.</ns0:note> have the keys of hell and of death <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">And have a Power to kill, and cast into Hell; or I have the Power over Death, and the state of the Dead, so as I can raise those that are dead, to life again; I have the command of Death, whether Temporal or Eternal; as he who hath the Keys of an House can let in, and shut out of it whom he pleaseth, so I bring to Heaven, and throw to Hell whom I please.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">19 Write the things which thou hast seen <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Either the things which thou hast seen from the be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ginning of the Gospel; for <ns0:hi>Iohn,</ns0:hi> Ma<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. 4.21. was a Compa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nion of Christ from the time presently following his <ns0:hi>Baptism</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Temptations</ns0:hi>: Or, the Vision of me, which thou hast now had; which I judge most probably the sense, not under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />standing why our Lord should set <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> to write what (tho they were not yet written, yet) Christ knew, should be written in another Book by <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> himself, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> in his Gos<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pel, and by <ns0:hi>Matthew, Mark,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Luke,</ns0:hi> in their Histories of the Gospel, and in the <ns0:hi>Acts of the Apostles,</ns0:hi> especially consi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dering they were to be wrote plainly, so as he who runs may read them; and what <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> was to write here, was to be written <ns0:hi>Enigmatically,</ns0:hi> and darkly represented in Vi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sions: and it is against reason to think the same things should be first revealed plainly, and then more darkly, and both by Direction from God.</ns0:note>, and the things which are <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">The present Affairs of the Church; we have the History till <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> was carried Prisoner to <ns0:hi>Rome,</ns0:hi> (which was about the 60th year after Christ) in the <ns0:hi>Acts of the Apostles</ns0:hi>; so that I conceive the furthest that <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> lookt back, was but 35 years; for he was in <ns0:hi>Patmos</ns0:hi> about 93, and is conceived to have wrote this Book, 96. Hence the mat<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter of the <ns0:hi>Revelation</ns0:hi> is easily concluded. 1. <ns0:hi>The things which were</ns0:hi> the present Affairs of the Church, <ns0:hi>Anno</ns0:hi> 96. or looking back only to 60, which Things are supposed to be written by <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> in <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 2.3.</ns0:note>, and the things which shall be hereafter <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">And <ns0:hi>the Things which shall be hereafter,</ns0:hi> to the end of the World, under the reign of the <ns0:hi>Dragon</ns0:hi> [the <ns0:hi>Pagan Roman</ns0:hi> Empire] and the reign of <ns0:hi>Anti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />christ,</ns0:hi> or the <ns0:hi>Beast,</ns0:hi> for 1260 years, and from thence until Christ shall come to Judgment.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">20 The mystery of the seven stars which thou sawest in my right hand, and the seven golden candlesticks <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">See <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 12, 16.</ns0:note>. The seven stars are <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mal. 2.7<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                  </ns0:note> the angels of the seven churches <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">That is, they signifie the <ns0:hi>Angels of the seven Churches.</ns0:hi> By <ns0:hi>Angels,</ns0:hi> he means God's Messengers and Em<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bassadors to the <ns0:hi>seven Churches,</ns0:hi> called <ns0:hi>Angels,</ns0:hi> both in respect of their <ns0:hi>Office,</ns0:hi> being the Embassadors of Christ, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 5. 20. and of that <ns0:hi>Holiness</ns0:hi> which they should shew forth in their Doctrine and Life. To interpret the term of <ns0:hi>Angels</ns0:hi> by Nature, seems not agreeable to what we shall hereafter meet with, said to some of them, Christ would never have ordered <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> to have charged them with <ns0:hi>a loss of their first love,</ns0:hi> or to admonish them to be <ns0:hi>faithful unto Death,</ns0:hi> or to <ns0:hi>repent.</ns0:hi> Whether the term, <ns0:hi>Angel,</ns0:hi> denoteth any particular superior Minister, or <ns0:hi>Bishop</ns0:hi> in those Churches, or is to be taken <ns0:hi>collectively</ns0:hi> for all the Ministers in those Churches, I shall not dispute. Certain it is, <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> signifieth no more than is common to all Ministers, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> to be <ns0:hi>God</ns0:hi>'s <ns0:hi>Messengers,</ns0:hi> and move upon his Errand.</ns0:note>; and the seven candlesticks which thou sawest, are the seven churches <ns0:note n="*" place="bottom">The seven Churches mention<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 11. Or else, seven being the Number of Perfection, all the Churches, which are fitly represented by <ns0:hi>Candle<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sticks,</ns0:hi> in the same sense as they are called <ns0:hi>Pillars of Truth</ns0:hi> in <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi>'s Epistle to <ns0:hi>Timothy,</ns0:hi> because they have not the Light they shew from themselves, only hold it forth from Christ. But<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> it is the Opinion of very learned Writers upon this Book, That our Lord, by these <ns0:hi>seven Churches,</ns0:hi> signifies all the Churches of Christ to the end of the World; and by what he saith to them, designs to shew what shall be the state of the Churches in all Ages, and what their Duty is. That by the Church of <ns0:hi>Ephesus,</ns0:hi> was represented the purest state of all the Christian Churches, which determined 30 years be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore this Book was wrote. By the <ns0:hi>Church of Smyrna,</ns0:hi> the state of all Christian Churches till the year 300. By the <ns0:hi>Church of Pergamos,</ns0:hi> all the Christian Churches, till Anti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />christ got up into the Saddle, and the <ns0:hi>Albigenses,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Wal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />denses</ns0:hi> were so persecuted. 4. By the <ns0:hi>Church of Thy<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>tira,</ns0:hi> the state of the Churches from that time, till our Reforma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion. 5. By the other three, the state of all Churches for 150 years last past, and which shall be to the end of the World. See Dr. <ns0:hi>More,</ns0:hi> Mr. <ns0:hi>Med<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>, Cocceius,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Forbes,</ns0:hi> as learn<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed and diligent Enquirers into the Sense of this Book, as any have been, give many reasons for this: 1. Because no reason else can be given, why Epistles should not be wrote to other Churches, as well as these. 2. He doth not call them the seven Churches of <ns0:hi>Asia,</ns0:hi> but seven Churches. 3. The Number, seven, is a Number used to signifie Perfection. 4. What is said of Christ's walking in the midst <ns0:hi>of the Gol<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />den Candlesticks</ns0:hi> having the <ns0:hi>Stars in his Right Hand,</ns0:hi> &c. agreeth to him, with reference to all <ns0:hi>Churches,</ns0:hi> not to these seven only. 5. His calling Ministers, <ns0:hi>Angels,</ns0:hi> speaks this a Prophecy, for that is a Prophetical stile. 6. The mention<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing the same Number of Churches and Ministers, as of the Seals, speaks this part of the Revelation as comprehensive, with respect to time, as the other. 7. It is not probable, that these Epistles would have been ushered in with such a Vision, if they had been meerly Historical, and Didactick, not Prophetical also. 8. They argue from <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 1.19. where <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> is bid to write not only <ns0:hi>what is,</ns0:hi> but <ns0:hi>what shall come to pass.</ns0:hi> 9. They argue from the matter of the Epistles.—Let the curious Reader see more of this in the Authors themselves, as also in Mr. <ns0:hi>Brightman.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
